title: The Bijagós to the Plaza: Benkos Biohó, the Arcabuco, and the Free Town of Palenque
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bijagós Islands, the birth
stops.date_confidence: Undocumented. English Wikipedia gives only 'late 16th century'; Spanish Wikipedia a range of roughly c.1550-1599. No source states a birth year, and the widely quoted 1550 sits at the extreme early edge of that range. The pin year is a nominal placeholder inside the range. Ethnicity contradicted between editions: Spanish says Bijago, English says Mandinka of royal lineage; not resolved.
stops.campa: Off the Guinea coast the Bijagós lie scattered in shallow water, islands of mangrove and rice ground whose people the Portuguese on the mainland have never subdued. Into one of them a boy is born to a family that the tradition of Palenque remembers as royal; no register anywhere sets down his name or his year. He grows up in a country where a king is a man the villages consent to follow, and where the sea is a road rather than a wall. The Portuguese factors at the river mouths are already buying and shipping his neighbours by the head.
suggested_refs: The Bijagós archipelago and its stateless island polities in the late sixteenth century

stops.name: Cacheu, the fort at the river mouth
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source places Biohó at Cacheu by name; the fort is included as the necessary route between the Bijagós and the Atlantic trade. The year is nominal, taken as shortly before the 1596 sale at Cartagena that Spanish Wikipedia does attest.
stops.campa: The Cacheu river runs brown out of the mainland forest, and at its mouth the Portuguese keep a stockade, warehouses, a chapel and a pen. Everything taken from the Bijagós and the Casamance passes through here to be counted, priced and branded before it goes aboard. The asiento holders in Lisbon and Seville buy their licences by the head and sell the heads on. Every road from his islands to the ocean runs past this fort. No ledger names the man later called Benkos Biohó among the people held at Cacheu in these years.
suggested_refs: The Portuguese praça of Cacheu, principal slaving depot of the Guinea rivers
sources: General historiography of the Cacheu slave trade; Biohó's presence there is not attested by any source

stops.name: The Atlantic crossing, under Reynel's licence
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the coordinate is a nominal mid-ocean marker corresponding to no documented position: no source records the vessel, its route, or any point of the crossing. Pedro Gómez Reynel held the Crown's asiento rather than personally shipping captives. The wife Wiwa and the children Sando and Orika are Spanish-language tradition, not documented at sea.
stops.campa: He crosses in the hold of a ship licensed under the contract Pedro Gómez Reynel holds from the Spanish crown, the monopoly that supplies the Indies with African captives at so many pesos a head. Spanish tradition puts his wife Wiwa in the same hold, and their children Sando and Orika. Weeks of dark and salt water lie between the Cacheu bar and the American coast, and the trade expects to lose a share of its cargo on the way and prices accordingly. He arrives alive.
suggested_refs: The asiento of Pedro Gómez Reynel, 1595-1600, for the supply of captives to the Indies

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the landing
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Spanish and English Wikipedia, which give 1596 for both the enslavement by Reynel and the sale at Cartagena; the month and day are unknown and default to 01-01. The pin is the atlas canonical Cartagena coordinate rather than the colonial mole, whose exact site is not attested for this landing.
stops.campa: The ship comes in past Bocachica into the finest harbour on the Spanish Main, and Cartagena de Indias takes delivery. This is the licensed door through which Africa enters South America: the captives are landed, washed, oiled, and examined by surgeons acting for buyers in Peru and New Granada before they are sold. He is property twice traded here, bought by the merchant Juan de Palacio and passed on to Captain Alonso de Campos, whose name some records give as Alonso del Campo. Which of the two forms the notary wrote is no longer recoverable.
suggested_refs: The licensed slave port of Cartagena de Indias, chief entrepot of the Spanish Main

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the slave market
stops.date_confidence: The sale year is attested; the month is arbitrary, placed after the landing. The market's siting at what is now the Plaza de los Coches rests on general historiography of the city and is not attested for Biohó's sale in particular.
stops.campa: The market stands a few steps inside the wall, on the square where the carriages wait now, with the sea audible over the roofs. He learns Castilian here, and the shape of the city: its gates, its garrison, its water, its roads inland. The colony believes it is training a useful servant, and is walking a man from the Bijagós through the working parts of a fortified port. Around him the buyers pace the rows, the notaries write out the deeds, and the priests baptise what has been sold.
suggested_refs: The colonial slave market of Cartagena, on the ground of the present Plaza de los Coches
sources: General historiography of the Cartagena slave market

stops.name: The lower Magdalena, the boat goes down
stops.date_confidence: Undated in every source consulted. English Wikipedia records the sinking and the recapture with no year; the commonly quoted 1598 appears nowhere. The date is a placeholder between the 1596 sale and the 1599 flight. The coordinate is a nominal point on the lower Magdalena: no source locates the wreck.
stops.campa: He is put aboard a boat on the great river that carries everything the colony owns toward the interior, and the boat goes down. In the confusion he gets clear, into bank country of cane and mud where a swimmer can vanish inside a minute. He is taken again. The river has shown him what he needed to know: that the swamp is not Spanish ground, that a column cannot follow a man into it, and that the colony's grip ends where the water starts. What is done to him after the recapture no source records.
suggested_refs: The Magdalena river route between Cartagena and the interior of New Granada

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the flight of the thirty
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the year by both Wikipedia editions and by Simón, who places the rising 'en estos tiempos' around the turn of the governorship of Jerónimo de Suazo, which he dates to the end of 1599 or the beginning of 1600. The month is inferred from that phrasing, not documented. The number thirty is traditional.
stops.campa: By the end of 1599 he goes for good, and he does not go alone. Some thirty people leave the city with him, out past the last houses into the ciénaga country to the southeast where horses founder and columns lose the trail. Fray Pedro Simón, writing the chronicle of Tierra Firme a generation later, sets the beginning of the trouble in the first days of Don Jerónimo de Suazo's governorship and gives it a word the Spanish will use for the next two hundred years.
stops.quote: comenzó un alzamiento y retiro de ciertos negros cimarrones
stops.quote_source: Fray Pedro Simón, Noticias historiales, Tomo V, Séptima Noticia Historial, cap. XXII, p. 219 (Bogotá, 1892)
suggested_refs: Simón, Noticias historiales, Séptima Noticia Historial, cap. XXII, on the rising of the cimarrones
sources: Fray Pedro Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme en las Indias Occidentales, Tomo V, Bogota: Medardo Rivas, 1892 (archive.org, tierrafirmeindias05simbrich)

stops.name: The marshes southeast of Cartagena, the band forms
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline by both Wikipedia editions, which place the fugitives in swampland southeast of the city; the coordinate is a regional marker for that marsh country rather than a documented camp, and the year is nominal for the months after the flight.
stops.campa: The swamp behind Cartagena is black water, cane, mosquito and mangrove root, crossable on foot only by people who have learned it. Here the thirty become a band and the band becomes a command. He divides them, sets watches on the trails, sends some back toward the city to carry word to the enslaved still inside it, and starts the practice that will feed the settlement for twenty years: every raid brings people out. The Spanish call them cimarrones, which is the word they use for cattle gone wild in the hills.
suggested_refs: The ciénaga country southeast of Cartagena, first refuge of the 1599 fugitives

stops.name: Montes de María, the death of Juan Gómez
stops.date_confidence: The engagement is attested by en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque', which records a first expedition of twenty armed men defeated and its leader Juan Gómez killed. No source locates the fight or dates it; the coordinate is a nominal Montes de María marker and the year is inferred from the sequence.
stops.campa: Cartagena sends twenty armed men under Juan Gómez to bring the runaways back. The cimarrones let the column into ground of their own choosing and break it there, and Gómez is killed. It is the first military fact of the palenque's existence, and it travels faster than any decree: on the estates around Tolú and along the Dique it is now known that the swamp people beat soldiers. The governor's next expedition will have to be larger, and the one after that larger again. Recruits follow the news in.
suggested_refs: The first Spanish expedition against the palenque, twenty men under Juan Gómez

stops.name: La Matuna, the first settlement
stops.date_confidence: Placement contradicted between Spanish-language sources and not resolved: es.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque' puts La Matuna in marshland near the present Canal del Dique, roughly 10.1 to 10.2 N, while es.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó' puts it south of Tolú, roughly 9.67 N, some 70 km away. The northern reading is pinned here. The date is nominal.
stops.campa: They settle in the marshland the sources call la Matuna, and for a while the community carries that name. What recommends the place is water on the approaches, cane thick enough to hide a village, and one path in that a handful of men can hold. Wiwa is with him. Fugitives come in from the estates along the Dique and are taken up, on the one condition that they can be trusted, and the settlement grows a good deal faster than the governor in Cartagena is told.
suggested_refs: The marshes of la Matuna, first name of the community that became San Basilio de Palenque

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the stakes driven
stops.date_confidence: The year 1603 is the founding date cut into the town's own monument, not a documentary date; no source dates the founding. English Wikipedia further states there is no direct documentary relationship between Biohó and this specific modern municipality, only a palenque of the same tradition in the same hills; the contradiction with Spanish sources and local memory is left open.
stops.campa: On rising ground in the Montes de María the settlement builds itself a wall: driven stakes, a ditch, thorn packed between, the palenque that gives the place and every place like it its name. Inside are houses, ground broken for yuca and maize, a plaza. The hills behind offer retreat and the ridges offer sight lines down to the coastal plain. Nothing in the work suggests a hiding place; it is laid out to be held. The town's monument cuts 1603 into its base as the year of the founding.
suggested_refs: The palisade earthworks of the Montes de María palenques

stops.name: Palenque de San Miguel Arcángel, the naming
stops.date_confidence: Contradicted and not resolved: en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque' says the village was first known as Palenque de San Miguel Arcángel, while es.wikipedia says it was initially called palenque de la Matuna. The date is nominal for the early years of the settlement. The later name San Basilio belongs to the eighteenth century, itself dated 1713 in English and 1714 in Spanish.
stops.campa: The place is called Palenque de San Miguel Arcángel, after the archangel painted in every church on this coast standing on the neck of the devil with a drawn sword. Other accounts keep the older name, la Matuna, after the marsh they came out of. A Spanish saint's name on a free black town inside a Catholic empire is not a concession to anybody; it is a claim to standing, made in the empire's own vocabulary. San Basilio, the name the town carries now, is a hundred years off.
suggested_refs: The cult of Saint Michael the Archangel on the Caribbean coast of New Granada

stops.name: The Montes de María, rey del Arcabuco
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and later than it appears. The title rey del Arcabuco is absent from en.wikipedia; in es.wikipedia it traces to Camilo Delgado's legend 'El Rey del Arcabuco', published in 1913 in Historia, leyendas y tradiciones de Cartagena. It is a twentieth-century literary coinage absorbed into the historical account, not a contemporary title. The coordinate is a regional anchor in the Montes de María; the year is nominal.
stops.campa: He takes a title. Arcabuco is the word on this coast for tangled hill forest that horses cannot enter and no surveyor has ever drawn, and he calls himself its king. The kingship is measured by what his people actually hold: the trails, the water, the passes down to the plain, the estates that pay him in silence rather than be burned. In the city he is a runaway with a price on his head. A king in this country is a man the villages consent to follow, which is what he was born to and what he has rebuilt three thousand miles from where he learned it.
suggested_refs: Camilo Delgado, 'El Rey del Arcabuco', in Historia, leyendas y tradiciones de Cartagena (1913)
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Camilo Delgado' / Delgado, Historia, leyendas y tradiciones de Cartagena (1913)

stops.name: The palenque, the offices of government
stops.date_confidence: The offices are attested by es.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó': a captain general named Lorencillo, a lieutenant of war, a chief constable, a treasurer. Neither the seat nor any date is documented; the coordinate is a nominal point in the palenque's hill country and the year is arbitrary within the settlement's armed decade.
stops.campa: He governs with offices. A captain general named Lorencillo commands the fighters; under him a lieutenant of war, a chief constable, a treasurer. Sentries stand fixed rotations, prisoners are handled by rule, the paths in are watched day and night. The whole apparatus mirrors the colonial government forty miles away, post for post, and every man holding one of these posts was somebody's property a few years ago. Nothing of it was written down at the palenque's end; the offices are known because the Spanish kept the names.
suggested_refs: The military and civil offices of the Montes de María palenque under Biohó

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the hinterland ungovernable
stops.date_confidence: Attested in general terms by both Wikipedia editions, which record repeated Spanish expeditions repelled over more than a decade; no individual expedition after Juan Gómez is named or dated in the sources consulted, and the year is a nominal placement before the 1605 peace offer.
stops.campa: They come within sight of the walls. The estates on the approaches to Cartagena are burned and stripped, the roads out of the city are unsafe after dark, and the governor writes to Spain about a black king in the hills who has made the hinterland of the empire's chief Caribbean port ungovernable. The crown is paying, year on year, for a war against people it still legally owns. Expedition after expedition marches into the Montes de María and comes back thinner.
suggested_refs: Spanish punitive expeditions from Cartagena into the Montes de María, 1600-1605

stops.name: Santiago de Tolú, the coast raided
stops.date_confidence: Tolú is named among the raid targets by es.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó'; no individual raid is dated or narrated in any source, so the year is a nominal placement inside the raiding decade.
stops.campa: Santiago de Tolú sits on the Gulf of Morrosquillo with its cattle grounds and its landing for the coasting trade, and the cimarrones come down on it out of the hills. They take arms, powder, cattle, tools, the iron that a settlement in the forest cannot make for itself. They also take people, in the raiders' sense of the word: the enslaved of the district are carried off into the arcabuco, and few of them argue about it on the way. The town rebuilds, writes to Cartagena for a garrison it does not get, and is raided again.
suggested_refs: Santiago de Tolú and the cattle estates of the Gulf of Morrosquillo

stops.name: Santa Cruz de Mompox, the river port struck
stops.date_confidence: Mompós is named among the raid targets by es.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó'. No raid on it is dated or described in any source consulted; the year is nominal.
stops.campa: Mompox lies far up the Magdalena, the river port where the silver and the hides and the merchandise of a whole viceroyalty change boats. Raiding parties out of the Montes de María reach it. The distance is the argument: a governor can tell Madrid that runaways in a swamp are a local nuisance, but a force that strikes the colony's main artery two hundred miles inland is a war being lost. What the raiders took at Mompox, and on what day, is nowhere recorded; the town survives in the account as a name on a list of targets.
suggested_refs: The Magdalena river commerce between Mompox and Cartagena

stops.name: Tenerife, the Magdalena town taken
stops.date_confidence: Tenerife is named among the raid targets by es.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó'; the raid is undated and the year is nominal. Coordinate corrected to the town's own figure, 9 degrees 53 minutes 56 seconds N, 74 degrees 51 minutes 32 seconds W; a widely circulated 9.9422, -74.8506 sits about 5 km north of the town.
stops.campa: Tenerife on the lower Magdalena is another river town in the path, and the cimarrones take it in turn for arms, food and recruits. The pattern is set by now. The column comes out of the hills at night; the town wakes to find its powder gone and its enslaved people gone with it; the trail into the arcabuco is cold before any pursuit can be mounted, and the pursuit, when it goes out, is made up of men who do not want to be in that forest after dark. Fifteen years of this go by without a single Spanish expedition finding the palenque itself.
suggested_refs: Tenerife, Magdalena, and the river towns of the lower Magdalena

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the offer of Governor Suazo
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the exact day by both Wikipedia editions: 18 July 1605, Governor Jerónimo de Suazo y Casasola opens peace negotiations recognising the maroons' freedom. The place within the city is not specified in the sources; the canonical Cartagena pin is used.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of July the governor Jerónimo de Suazo y Casasola makes an offer no Spanish official on this coast has made before: peace with the palenque, and recognition of its people as free where they stand. Suazo has added up the cost of the expeditions and the cost of estates that no longer produce, and buying the war's end is the cheaper column. The paper treats the men in the arcabuco as a party capable of agreeing to something. Whether it ever reached them, and in whose hands, no document says.
suggested_refs: The peace overture of Jerónimo de Suazo y Casasola, 18 July 1605

stops.name: Montes de María, the years the offer does not hold
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Spanish Wikipedia indicates the 1605 offer was not implemented at once and that conflict and negotiation continued for years; no event in this interval is documented and no date within it is attested. The year is a midpoint marker between 1605 and the treaty.
stops.campa: The offer of 1605 does not become a peace. Raiding goes on, terms are argued and withdrawn, governors change in Cartagena, and the palenque keeps taking in fugitives, which is the single thing the crown will not concede. For the better part of a decade the two governments talk and fight at the same time, and neither stops doing either. Nothing from these years is written down at the palenque's end, and what survives is what the Spanish side chose to keep.
suggested_refs: The interval between the 1605 overture and the treaty under Fernández de Velasco

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the treaty of Fernández de Velasco
stops.date_confidence: Year contradicted three ways and not resolved: en.wikipedia gives 1612, es.wikipedia gives 1613, and Simón himself writes 'los años de 1612 ó 13'. All three name Governor Diego Fernández de Velasco. The month and day are unknown. Terms sometimes attached to this treaty, requiring Spanish dress and a sword or barring Biohó from royal titles, appear in no source and are not carried here.
stops.campa: Governor Diego Fernández de Velasco puts his name to the peace. The crown recognises the autonomy of the palenque; its people are licensed to enter Cartagena and to leave it as they please, going in and out with their captain Dominguillo at all hours. A free black town now exists inside the Spanish Indies by treaty, on paper, signed by the king's own governor. Fray Pedro Simón, recording it a generation later, calls it a bad peace that afterwards was made better. English sources date the treaty to 1612, Spanish sources to 1613, and Simón hedges between the two.
stops.quote: salieron de una mala paz, que después se vino á hacer mejor y á darles licencia para que entrasen en la ciudad y saliesen de ella con su Capitán Dominguillo, como lo hacían á todas horas
stops.quote_source: Fray Pedro Simón, Noticias historiales, Tomo V, Séptima Noticia Historial, cap. XXIII, pp. 223-224 (Bogotá, 1892)
suggested_refs: The treaty of Diego Fernández de Velasco with the palenque, 1612 or 1613
sources: Fray Pedro Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme en las Indias Occidentales, Tomo V, Bogota: Medardo Rivas, 1892 (archive.org, tierrafirmeindias05simbrich)

stops.name: The streets of Cartagena, the gilded dagger
stops.date_confidence: The manner of his appearance in the city is attested by Simón, quoted here; no individual visit is dated and the year is a nominal placement inside the period the peace held. Note that the dress and the sword are Simón's description of his bearing, not, as is often stated, conditions of the treaty.
stops.campa: He walks in through the gate he was once carried through in irons, and he walks in dressed. The licence in the treaty lets the people of the palenque enter the city and leave it at all hours, and he comes in under it. Doublet and hose in the Spanish cut, a sword at the hip, a gilded dagger, and the carriage of a caballero: this is how Fray Pedro Simón, who is no admirer, describes him in the streets of Cartagena during the years the peace holds. Simón's word for the bearing is arrogancia. Men who bought and sold him step aside for him on the pavement.
stops.quote: y el Bioho andaba con tanta arrogancia, que demás de andar bien vestido á la española, con espada y daga dorada, trataba su persona como un gran caballero
stops.quote_source: Fray Pedro Simón, Noticias historiales, Tomo V, Séptima Noticia Historial, cap. XXIII, pp. 223-224 (Bogotá, 1892); spelling as printed in the 1892 edition
suggested_refs: Simón, Noticias historiales, cap. XXIII, on Biohós bearing in Cartagena
sources: Fray Pedro Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme en las Indias Occidentales, Tomo V, Bogota: Medardo Rivas, 1892 (archive.org, tierrafirmeindias05simbrich)

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, taken at the wall
stops.date_confidence: The year 1619 is attested by both Wikipedia editions; the month and day are unknown. English Wikipedia has him seized while walking into the city, Spanish Wikipedia at the city wall, unguarded. Simón, the earliest source, does not describe an arrest at all and instead has Biohó hanged in 1619.
stops.campa: They take him at the wall. He comes in as the treaty allows, unguarded, on a day like the days before it, and the guard closes around him. The safe conduct he is walking under was signed six years earlier by the crown's own governor. Governor García Girón's justification is not that Biohó has broken the peace; it is that he is believed in too widely, and his standing among the Africans of the city and the coast makes him, in the governor's judgment, too dangerous to leave alive.
suggested_refs: The safe conduct of the 1612 or 1613 treaty, broken in 1619

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the two years unaccounted for
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and an empty interval. No source documents a holding site, conditions, a trial, or any event between the 1619 arrest and the 1621 execution; the custody is inferred from the gap between two dates. Simón's dating of the execution to 1619 would remove the interval altogether.
stops.campa: He is held in the city. Where, under what conditions, and whether anything resembling a trial takes place, no surviving document says. The record has his seizure at one end and his killing at the other and nothing whatever in between, which is two years of a man's life that nobody wrote down. In the hills the palenque does not surrender, does not march on Cartagena, and does not disperse. Why the governor waits so long, and what the palenque is doing while he waits, is a question the archive leaves standing.
suggested_refs: The gap in the record between the arrest of 1619 and the execution of 1621

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, hanged and quartered
stops.date_confidence: The date 16 March 1621, the method, and the ordering governor García Girón are attested by both Wikipedia editions. Contradicted at source: Simón, the earliest narrative, says Biohó was hanged in 1619, also by García Girón. Not resolved. The square is not named by either Wikipedia edition; identifying it as the Plaza Mayor or the present Plaza de la Aduana is unsourced inference, so the canonical Cartagena pin is used.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of March they hang him in the square and then quarter the body, the punishment the empire keeps for rebellion, designed from end to end to be watched. The audience is the enslaved population of Cartagena, several thousand strong, brought or drawn to see what the end of a black king looks like. Forty miles inland in the hills, the palenque does not move. García Girón has the corpse and he has the ceremony. Fray Pedro Simón, the earliest narrative source, puts the hanging two years earlier than this, in 1619, and by the same governor.
suggested_refs: Spanish colonial punishment for rebellion: hanging followed by quartering
sources: Fray Pedro Simon, Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme en las Indias Occidentales, Tomo V, Bogota: Medardo Rivas, 1892 (archive.org, tierrafirmeindias05simbrich)

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the remains unaccounted for
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. Display of the quartered parts is standard Spanish colonial practice, but no source names where Biohós remains were set, for how long, or what became of them. The date is the day after the execution and is a marker only.
stops.campa: Quartering exists in order to be exhibited. The parts of a rebel's body go up at the gates and along the roads out of the city, where everyone coming in to market has to pass them, and they stay there until the weather and the birds take them down. He has no grave, nothing of him under the statue at Palenque and nothing of him in Cartagena. No document names where Biohó's remains were set, or for how long, or what became of them afterwards, and no chronicler thought the question worth an answer.
suggested_refs: The colonial practice of displaying quartered remains at city gates
sources: General practice of quartering executions in Spanish colonial Cartagena; no source names the display sites for Biohó

stops.name: Montes de María, the palenque holds
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from the documented continuity of the settlement into the eighteenth century; no event is attested for this year, which is a marker for the decades between the execution and the royal decree of 1691.
stops.campa: The town keeps its wall and keeps taking people in. Governors come and go in Cartagena, the estates along the Dique go on losing workers into the Montes de María, and the expeditions grow rarer and then stop coming altogether. Nobody in Cartagena sets down what the town is doing through these decades, and the palenque itself writes nothing. A generation grows up inside the palisade that has never seen the city and never worn anyone's iron. They speak a language nobody in Cartagena can follow.
suggested_refs: The survival of the Montes de María palenque through the seventeenth century

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the royal decree of 1691
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque': a royal decree guaranteeing the community's freedom on condition it stop harbouring new runaways. The month and day are unknown.
stops.campa: The crown issues a decree guaranteeing the freedom of the people of the palenque, on one condition: that they stop receiving runaways. It is the same condition every Spanish offer has carried since 1605, and it is the one term the palenque has never once kept, because keeping it would mean turning away the people it was built for. Fugitives go on arriving from the estates along the Dique and go on being taken in, and the population grows through the whole of the century that follows. Madrid has conceded the principle and left the practice where it found it.
suggested_refs: The royal decree of 1691 on the freedom of the palenque

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the agreement of Bishop Casiani
stops.date_confidence: Contradicted and not resolved. en.wikipedia 'Benkos Biohó' calls the 1713 instrument a royal decree making San Basilio the first free village of the Americas; en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque' describes it as an agreement signed by Bishop Antonio María Casiani in January 1713 granting conditional land rights, with 137 houses counted; es.wikipedia dates the decree establishing the name San Basilio to 1714. The day within January is unknown.
stops.campa: Bishop Antonio María Casiani signs an agreement in January: land rights for the community, conditional as always on turning away new fugitives. Colombia has remembered this instrument ever since as the act that made San Basilio the first free town of the Americas, and quarrels in the footnotes about whether it was a royal decree or a bishop's bargain, and whether the year was 1713 or 1714. A count made that year finds one hundred and thirty-seven houses standing where the palisade was.
suggested_refs: The Casiani agreement of January 1713 and the count of 137 houses

stops.name: Mahates, the jurisdiction closes over it
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque': formal incorporation into the jurisdiction of Mahates under continuing restrictions against sheltering maroons. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: In 1772 the settlement is written into the jurisdiction of Mahates, the old restriction against sheltering maroons attached to the act, and passes from a country the empire could not enter into a line of provincial administration. There is no storming and no surrender. The war ends with a clerk, a boundary and a schedule of assessments. The town keeps its language and its kuagros, buries its dead the way it has always buried them, and begins paying its taxes to the district.
suggested_refs: The 1772 incorporation of San Basilio into the jurisdiction of Mahates

stops.name: The Canal del Dique, the road that passed it by
stops.date_confidence: The channel's proximity to the town is attested by en.wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque'; the date is a nominal marker for the colonial and republican centuries and no event is claimed for it. The coordinate is a point on the channel near the town rather than a specific site.
stops.campa: The artificial channel cut between the Magdalena and the bay of Cartagena runs a few miles from the town, carrying the colony's freight past its door. The palenque grew up in the angle between that traffic and the hills, near enough to strike the route and far enough that nobody with cargo aboard wanted to go looking for it. The geography that made the place a base later made it a backwater, a village on a bad road well off the highway. Its language is still spoken there.
suggested_refs: The Canal del Dique between the Magdalena river and Cartagena bay

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the written afterlife
stops.date_confidence: The three works and their dates are attested by es.wikipedia: Camilo Delgado's legend 'El Rey del Arcabuco' (1913), Germán Espinosa's 'Orika de los palenques' (1991), Antonio Prada Fortul's 'Benkos, las alas de un cimarrón' (2023). Corrected from a common error: the Espinosa piece is a short story, not a novel; his 1991 novel was La tragedia de Belinda Elsner, on an unrelated subject. The stop is dated to the earliest of the three.
stops.campa: The written afterlife begins late, and in fiction. In 1913 Camilo Delgado publishes 'El Rey del Arcabuco' among his legends and traditions of Cartagena, and the title fastens to Biohó so firmly that it is now quoted as though a Spanish clerk had set it down in 1610. Germán Espinosa gives Orika, the daughter of the tradition, a story of her own in 1991. Antonio Prada Fortul publishes Benkos, las alas de un cimarrón in 2023. Between the execution in the square and the first of those three books lie two hundred and ninety-two years in which nobody wrote a book about him at all.
suggested_refs: Delgado (1913), Espinosa (1991) and Prada Fortul (2023) on Biohó and the palenque

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the statue in the plaza
stops.date_confidence: The statue and its inscribed founding date of 1603 are attested by Spanish and English Wikipedia; the sculptor and the year of unveiling are not established in any source reached, and the date given here is a nominal twentieth-century marker. English Wikipedia's statement that no direct documentary relationship links Biohó to this municipality stands in flat contradiction to the monument and is not resolved.
stops.campa: In the plaza he stands in bronze with his arms open and his chains broken, and 1603 is cut into the base as the year of the founding. The town has never needed a piece of paper to know whose town it is. Professional historians point out that no surviving document links the man executed in Cartagena in 1621 to this particular village, only to a palenque of the same generation in the same hills. The statue does not answer them. Which of the two the bronze commemorates is a question the record leaves open.
suggested_refs: The monument to Benkos Biohó in the plaza of San Basilio de Palenque, inscribed 1603

stops.name: Parque Apolo, Cartagena, the second figure
stops.date_confidence: The existence of a monument to Biohó in the Parque Apolo at Cartagena is attested by es.wikipedia; the sculptor, the unveiling year and the park's own coordinates were not available in the sources reached, so the canonical Cartagena pin is used and the date is a nominal twentieth-century marker.
stops.campa: A second figure of him stands in Cartagena itself, in the Parque Apolo, in the city that bought him at market, hunted him for twenty years, treatied with him as a power, and killed him in its main square in front of everyone it still owned. The port that landed more African captives than any other on the Spanish Main now keeps a monument to the one man who got out of it, built a country in the hills behind it, and came back in through its own gate wearing a sword. Nobody has recorded who made the statue, or when it went up.
suggested_refs: The monument to Benkos Biohó at Parque Apolo, Cartagena de Indias

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the language
stops.date_confidence: Palenquero's description as the only creole in the Americas with a Spanish lexicon and Bantu grammatical structure, chiefly Kikongo, is attested by UNESCO element 00102. The lumbalú and the mapalé are documented in English and Spanish Wikipedia 'San Basilio de Palenque', not in the UNESCO element description. The date is the year of the UNESCO proclamation.
stops.campa: The town speaks Palenquero: Spanish words carried on Bantu grammar, chiefly Kikongo, the only creole of its kind in the Americas. It is what the first generation behind the palisade built out of the languages they arrived with and the language of the men who sold them. When somebody dies the lumbalú begins, nine days of drums and mourning songs called up by a rhythm that everyone in the village can recognise from the far end of the street. None of it is staged for visitors, though visitors come. The mapalé is danced with the hips and the shoulders, and it is danced fast.
suggested_refs: Palenquero, the lumbalú funerary ceremony, and the mapalé
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, element 00102, 'Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio'

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the UNESCO listing
stops.date_confidence: The 2005 proclamation as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and the 2008 inscription on the Representative List at the Committee's third session are both attested by UNESCO element 00102. These are two administrative stages of one recognition; sources cite them inconsistently. The day given is the date of the third proclamation of Masterpieces and is not separately confirmed for this element.
stops.campa: UNESCO proclaims the Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and three years later the designation is folded into the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The same documentation records that the community's distinctiveness still draws stereotyping and discrimination in Colombia, and names that pressure among the threats to the survival of the practice being honoured.
suggested_refs: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element 00102, 'Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio'
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, element 00102, 'Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio'

stops.name: San Basilio de Palenque, the ma kuagro
stops.date_confidence: The kuagro system is attested by UNESCO element 00102 as age-based groups coordinating collective labour and life-cycle events. The population figure of roughly 3,500 is from the same source. The date is the year of inscription on the Representative List and marks the documentation, not the practice, which is undated.
stops.campa: Everyone born within a certain stretch of years belongs to a kuagro, and belongs to it for life. The kuagro works the ground together, builds together, buries its dead together, and answers collectively for the conduct of its members. It is the structure by which a besieged settlement organised its labour and its defence, still running in a town of some three and a half thousand people that has not been besieged in three hundred years. Children are placed in one before they can walk.
suggested_refs: The ma kuagro age-set organisation of San Basilio de Palenque
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, element 00102, 'Cultural Space of Palenque de San Basilio'
